clue.text: Male bird's mysterious plant

parts.note: a man is a male person
a drake is a male duck, a bird

explanation.surface: A naturalist reports that a male bird owns a strange plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The mandrake's forked root was credited with magic powers, hence 'mysterious'.
explanation.definitionFit: This narcotic herb with a forked root figured in folklore and witchcraft, so it is a plant with an air of mystery.

clue.text: One cadet who may be good for a story

indicators.note: the letters of these two words may be something else once rearranged

explanation.surface: A young officer cadet is said to be a good source of tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' signals that ONE CADET can be rearranged; 'who' and 'good for' only join.
explanation.definitionFit: An anecdote is a short personal story told in conversation.

clue.text: Devils on board? Right inside, it can be shown

parts.note: demons are devils

indicators.note: inside says the right letter goes within the word for board

parts.note: a table is a board, as in 'bed and board'

explanation.surface: Devils seated on a board are described as provable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Devils on board' paints imps on a table or ship; 'board' is furniture here. 'inside' places the right letter within it, and 'on' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that can be proved or exhibited is demonstrable.

clue.text: A puzzle for an angry parasite, say?

indicators.note: say tells us to speak the phrase and hear the result

parts.note: an angry parasite is a cross tick: cross is angry, a tick is a blood-sucking parasite

explanation.surface: Someone asks what puzzle suits a furious bloodsucker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks the homophone: 'a cross tick' spoken runs together as the puzzle word.
explanation.definitionFit: An acrostic is a word puzzle in which the initial letters of lines spell a word.

clue.text: The ban upsets me — to exclude the green light!

indicators.note: in a down clue, upsets turns the word me upside down, reading it from bottom to top

parts.note: to bar is to exclude
green on a traffic light means go

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a prohibition stops them getting permission to proceed.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'upsets' reads 'me' from bottom up. The exclamation makes 'green light' sound like permission refused, but it simply supplies the go signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An embargo is an official prohibition, especially on trade.

clue.text: Sally dismissed from the field

explanation.surface: A sortie and a dismissal are made on the same field.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman is run out when the stumps are broken before he reaches the crease, so he leaves the field.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a sudden dash out, a sortie; and a batsman so dismissed has been put out while running between wickets.

clue.text: The price of a ticket to the far East

parts.note: far is taken as written; that the letters also run across 'far East' is a coincidence of this charade, not a hidden word

explanation.surface: A traveller asks how much a ticket to the Far East costs.
explanation.definitionFit: A fare is the money a passenger pays for a journey.

clue.text: Throw (of course) out of a French joint

parts.note: un is the French for a
a saddle is a joint of meat, such as saddle of lamb

explanation.surface: A cook seems to be throwing a joint out of a French kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: '(of course)' means on a racecourse: a horse that throws its rider unseats him. 'out of' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: To unseat a jockey from a horse during a race is to throw the rider off.

clue.text: Mouse's mother visiting the Prophet?

parts.note: two sayings meet: in Horace a heaving peak gives birth to a ridiculous mouse, and the proverbial peak that would not come to Mohammed

explanation.surface: A mother mouse goes on a call to a holy man.
explanation.walkthrough: Horace's 'parturient montes, nascetur ridiculus mus' makes the great heap the mouse's parent; Bacon's proverb has Mohammed going to it since it would not come to him.
explanation.definitionFit: A high peak is both the parent of the mouse in Horace and the one that Mohammed had to visit.

clue.text: The start of one kind of measles

definitions.text: The start of one kind of measles

parts.words: The start of one kind of measles
parts.note: the word for the seed or origin of something is also the opening four letters of the name of rubella, the measles named after the country whose capital is Berlin

explanation.surface: A doctor describes the first sign of a particular measles infection.
explanation.walkthrough: Two readings: a beginning, and the first four letters of 'German' in German measles.
explanation.definitionFit: A germ is the origin or seed from which something grows, and a microbe that starts disease.

clue.text: Making a name, by the sound of it

definitions.text: Making a name, by the sound of it

parts.words: Making a name, by the sound of it
parts.note: the Greek roots mean name-making, and the figure forms words that imitate sounds

explanation.surface: Someone is apparently becoming famous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making a name' looks like winning fame; it is the literal Greek, onoma (name) plus poiein (make), for coining words like 'buzz' from sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: This figure of speech forms words that imitate the noise they describe, such as sizzle or cuckoo.

clue.text: No telescopes, but they bring the stars closer

definitions.text: No telescopes, but they bring the stars closer

parts.words: No telescopes, but they bring the stars closer
parts.note: the stars are performers on a stage, magnified by small binoculars used in a theatre

explanation.surface: Something that enlarges stars is said not to be a telescope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stars' suggests astronomy; they are singers seen from the stalls.
explanation.definitionFit: These small binoculars are used by audiences to see performers on stage more clearly.

clue.text: Sorted out the county

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are sorted out of their order and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone has finally sorted out the county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges SORTED. DORSET is a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: This shire on the south coast of England is one of its counties.

clue.text: There among the tribe assembled

indicators.note: among puts the first word inside the name of the tribe

parts.note: Gad was one of the twelve tribes of Israel

explanation.surface: A tribe has gathered there.
explanation.walkthrough: Gad, son of Jacob, founded one of the twelve tribes of Israel; 'among' sets the first word inside that name.
explanation.definitionFit: People who have come together in one place have assembled.

clue.text: Take away, being off the rails might one say?

indicators.note: might one say asks us to hear the made-up word spoken

parts.note: a train off the rails could be called de-tracked, taken off its track

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a derailed train is being taken away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might one say' marks a homophone of the coined word 'de-tracked'.
explanation.definitionFit: To detract is to take away from value or merit, as in 'detract from his achievement'.

clue.text: He is severely critical, if avuncular

definitions.text: He is severely critical, if avuncular

parts.words: He is severely critical, if avuncular
parts.note: a person who is uncle-like yet harsh is the man of the Netherlands in the idiom about frank, stern advice

explanation.surface: An uncle figure turns out to be harshly critical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Talk like a Dutch uncle' means to lecture someone sternly; 'avuncular' supplies the uncle.
explanation.definitionFit: A national of the Netherlands names the stern 'Dutch uncle' who rebukes candidly.

clue.text: Sideways with suspicion, look you!

parts.note: the word describes a distrustful sidelong glance, completing 'look ... at you'

explanation.surface: Someone tells another to glance sideways suspiciously.
explanation.walkthrough: The adverb goes with 'look': to look at someone this way is to eye them sidelong and with distrust.
explanation.definitionFit: Glancing askew with doubt or disapproval is looking this way, sidelong and mistrustfully.

clue.text: On the fiddle — in the bottom of the barrel?

definitions.text: in the bottom of the barrel

explanation.surface: A fiddler is cheating and has hit rock bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the fiddle' looks like fraud but means bowing a violin harshly; 'scraping the bottom of the barrel' is using the last poor resources.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing a violin badly is rasping at it with the bow; and in the idiom one is down to scraping the last dregs of a cask.

clue.text: Study an island for building material

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
Crete is a Greek island

explanation.surface: A student looks at an island as a source of building supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'con' meaning to study is old but common in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: This mix of cement, sand and gravel is a basic construction substance.

clue.text: Led the crew from the rear

definitions.text: Led the crew from the rear

parts.words: Led the crew from the rear
parts.note: in a racing eight the oarsman nearest the stern sets the pace, so he leads from the back of the boat

explanation.surface: A commander directs his men from behind the lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crew' suggests soldiers or sailors, but it is a rowing crew whose pace-setter sits at the stern.
explanation.definitionFit: The rower at the stern who sets the rhythm is the stroke; to do this job is a verb in past tense.

clue.text: Pet awkward baby with tact

indicators.note: awkward suggests the letters are clumsily jumbled

explanation.surface: Advice to handle a difficult baby tactfully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkward' rearranges BABY and TACT; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A striped domestic moggy is a common household animal kept for company.

clue.text: The flower of the universe

explanation.surface: Someone names the finest flower in all creation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower of' suggests 'the best of'; it is a garden plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A daisy-like garden plant of the aster family bears this name; and the ordered whole of creation is the other sense.

clue.text: Drawing the line with authority

explanation.surface: Someone in charge sets a firm limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawing the line' looks like setting a limit; it means ruling lines on paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Marking straight lines with a ruler is one sense; and a governing party or class holds power, the other.

clue.text: Presumably not the Act pleaded by Burke and Hare

definitions.text: Presumably not the Act pleaded by Burke and Hare

parts.words: Presumably not the Act pleaded by Burke and Hare
parts.note: the Latin name of the writ means 'you may have the body', a phrase grimly ironic for murderers who sold corpses

explanation.surface: A legal writ was hardly what two notorious killers relied on.
explanation.walkthrough: Burke and Hare were 1820s Edinburgh murderers who sold bodies to anatomists; a writ literally saying 'have the body' is the last thing they would invoke.
explanation.definitionFit: This writ demands that a detained person be brought before a court, protecting against unlawful imprisonment.

clue.text: Young resident at Buttercup Farm?

parts.note: Little Buttercup in HMS Pinafore confesses she practised infant-farming, nursing children for pay

explanation.surface: A youngster lives on a farm named after a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore, Little Buttercup sang that she ran a farm for infants and mixed two of them up.
explanation.definitionFit: An infant is a young child, the kind looked after on a so-called infant farm.

clue.text: It was St. Denis's first that was the difficult one

definitions.text: It was St. Denis's first that was the difficult one

parts.words: It was St. Denis's first that was the difficult one
parts.note: the saint walked carrying his own head, and Madame du Deffand said only the first pace costs anything

explanation.surface: A saint's first attempt was the hardest.
explanation.walkthrough: Legend says St Denis walked miles after beheading; Madame du Deffand remarked 'il n'y a que le premier pas qui coûte'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pace taken when walking is the single movement that the saint found hardest at the start.

clue.text: A classically white-hearted fish?

parts.note: alba is Latin, the classical tongue, for white
the core is the heart, so hearted gives the word for the centre

explanation.surface: A fish is described as white at its centre in classical terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'classically' points to Latin ALBA; 'A' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: This long-finned tuna of warm seas is a food fish.

clue.text: Did without a beau, having been taken in

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside puts the first word around the second

parts.note: taken as written
Beau Geste is the hero of P. C. Wren's Foreign Legion novel, so a beau suggests his surname

explanation.surface: Someone went without a boyfriend, having been fooled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is the old sense 'outside'. Beau Geste is P. C. Wren's 1924 Foreign Legion hero, so 'a beau' points to his surname. 'Taken in' looks like deceived but means absorbed.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that has been absorbed by the body, or ideas absorbed by the mind, have been assimilated.
